Document · 1992

An Interview Just Prior to the Release of Porco Rosso

Hayao Miyazaki · 1 August 1992
Animage, August, 1992 · from Starting Point: 1979–1996, Hayao Miyazaki (VIZ Media, 2009)

In the Whirlwind of an Era: Feeling stimulated by work

—Yesterday I had the privilege of watching the first screening of Porco Rosso with your staff, and I left with delightful memories of Fio Piccolo and the ladies who worked so hard at her father’s company, Piccolo S.P.A. This was especially so because in today’s world, people are always loudly demanding that their work hours be reduced, or that even public schools have both Saturday and Sunday off every week. I sensed that perhaps you were trying to send us a different message.

Miyazaki: No, there was no particular message. But I obviously believe that any true professional, if engaged in fulfilling work, will work as hard as he or she can. And I don’t think this is affected much by whether the hours are short or long. But I do hate it when people go around saying that people should sacrifice themselves for the sake of a corporation. Working hard for a corporation and working hard for the sake of one’s own profession are totally different things in my view.

Now, whether one person could really manage a sea plane factory like the Piccolo plant in Porco Rosso is of course a bit questionable. [laughs] But from what I’ve heard, Ryan Aeronautical Company, which built the plane Lindbergh used to cross the Atlantic, might have been somewhat similar. In those days, in little shops across America, some planes were being made by engineers drawing up blueprints on their own, working on a hunch, with a collection of ladies from the neighborhood doing the assembly. It was still a time when a person’s intuition, sense, experience, or even passion could have an overall effect on a plane’s performance. It’s an idea that I love, frankly. Now we’re in the high-tech age, and everything is made using computers.

—While making Porco Rosso, you yourself were obviously also running Studio Ghibli, an animation studio, so I wonder if that experience might also be reflected in the film.

Miyazaki: It would be great if, like Porco, I could sit around and smoke cigarettes while watching some young kid and making comments like, “Staying up late all the time’ll shorten your life,” or “It’ll be bad for your complexion.” [laughs] In the animated film, the men all run around acting stupid, and the women are all clever, hardworking, and reliable … What can I say, except that it’s a world such as you might find in the Japanese form of comic storytelling known as rakugo.

Of course, reality doesn’t work that way. It’d be pretty tough to live the way the characters in the film do. The staff members who worked on Porco Rosso had to burn the midnight oil all the time, and some didn’t even get to rest on Sunday. There are a lot of reasons for this, of course, and it’s an area where I need to make improvements, but I personally enjoy it when I become so absorbed in something that I completely forget about myself.

—It does seem as though that was reflected in your depiction of the late 1920s-style Piccolo seaplane factory.

Miyazaki: I think that the whole film really reflected the fact that to me, passion and effort are what working is all about. In the film, there’s a scene where Grandpa Piccolo says “Please forgive us, oh lord, for we are guilty of employing women’s hands to build this fighter plane,” and then laughs out loud, adding with a joyful expression, “Well, then, let’s load up on the grub so we can work like bees!” That’s it to me, that’s it. I think there’s a universal excitement that people experience when working.

Everyone thinks there are lots of jobs in today’s Japan, and they don’t get very passionate about their work, but in most countries around the world it’s the opposite—there aren’t enough jobs. There are probably more countries where people graduate from school only to find themselves unemployed.

People talk a lot about the collapse of the American economy, but I happen to think we’ll also witness the collapse of the Japanese economy soon. America switched from being a creditor nation to a debtor nation during World War II, and reached its peak in the 1950s. And it’s taken thirty or forty years to reach the state it’s in now. It’s taken far less time for the American economy to fall into the ruinous state it’s in than it did for the British economy to collapse after reaching its zenith in the Victorian era. As for the Soviet Union, well, even Imperial Russia lasted three hundred years.

In China, the Warring States and Spring and Autumn periods of history lasted five hundred years; five hundred years, despite the fact that there were huge strains on society, with terrible poverty and constant warfare. Compared to that, the socialist system in the Soviet Union only lasted seventy years, meaning that we’re seeing a tremendous acceleration of history.

Many people in Japan today are of the opinion that working all the time is a problem, but I happen to worry that in the near future so few people will work that it will become a problem. I think this is hinted at by the fact that so many people today just do the work they are told to do and are incapable of figuring out what they need to do beyond that. At the very minimum, I never want to lose the excitement I experience when I’m working. When I do, I think it’ll be all over for me.

No matter how messy things get, we’ve no choice but to live with vigor and courage

▶ At the turning point of an era

—Last summer, when production of Porco Rosso began in earnest, you did an interview for the Only Yesterday roman album, and in it you said something to the effect that, “We have come to a turning point in our era, but Porco Rosso is not a work on the cutting edge of that turning point; on the contrary it represents more of a ‘moratorium’ work.” Yet in viewing the film, I can’t help but think that some aspects of it do not fit into that category.

Miyazaki: I sensed that we had reached the turning point of an era when we began producing the film, but throughout the production I had no idea of what this really meant. Until then I had always thought that I made films with a good grasp of the era in which we live, but this was the least true this time. The film kept gradually getting longer (in the beginning Porco Rosso was supposed to be forty-five minutes, but it wound up being ninety minutes). But in making it, I had something of a realization.

—What kind of realization?

Miyazaki: Put quite simply, that “no matter how messy things get, we have no choice but to go on living.” In other words, up until the 1980s I think there was this view of the future that included an End Times. Japan would continue as is, get bigger and bigger, and then one day something would burst with a loud noise, and civilization would suddenly collapse. Or there might be a repeat of the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake in Tokyo, or everything might be turned into burned-out ruins. Of course, if this really happened, it would be a true disaster, a living hell, but if it were to happen, I think everyone also had this hope that they would feel cleansed. We were thinking a bit too naively and sweetly, in other words, even in the way we imagined things might all end.

At the beginning of 1990s, just when the Porco Rosso project got going, the Soviet Union collapsed, there was an escalation in ethnic conflict, we witnessed the start of people again starting to do all sorts of stupid things, and saw Japan’s economic bubble burst all around us. I came to realize that the End Times were not going to be as neat an affair as I had once imagined.

Even if problems we have now, such as atopic eczema and AIDS, run rampant, and even if the world’s population reaches ten billion, we’ll still have to go on living in a crush with everyone around us. There will have to be much more effort put into protecting the environment, and there will be, but the air will still be ever more polluted, and we’ll still have to go on living.

In other words, even if we’re surrounded by burned-out ruins, it won’t be possible to redo our urban planning, or to turn Tokyo into a beautiful new city. Even if we have an earthquake the size of the one that hit the Kanto plains in 1923, the buildings we have today won’t all fall down. The condo that Suzuki-san (the producer at Studio Ghibli) owns at Ebisu in Tokyo won’t collapse either. [laughs] So will it be possible to tear down all the old buildings and rebuild them? Probably not, because after a huge disaster no one will have any money. I suspect people would just keep living right here in the ruins, as is.

So that means most of Tokyo would turn into a slum. And if this were to be accompanied by the receding tide of a severe recession, all of a sudden the areas that used to be the liveliest in the city would go to ruin and become ghost towns, or turn into little Harlems. Some people may think that typhoons aren’t so bad because when one comes, it is followed by a flood, and after the waters have receded the sun will emerge in a blue sky and all will be sparkling clean and dandy. But it doesn’t work that way. Nothing’s sparkling clean after a typhoon passes. Yet I do suspect that we’ll see something like this is happen.

Heading into the twenty-first century, nothing’s been resolved. Everything’s being dragged into the new era, so we’ll just have to go on living, repeating the same stupid mistakes over and over again. That’s the realization I’ve had.

—So what you’re saying is that ultimately, in this context, you’ll just have to keep doing what you’ve been doing, keep struggling and muddling through.

Miyazaki: What we call the “bubble” period in Japan was, I think, a bloated and carefree era. It was a time when people were quite giddy about the future, and it was possible to take time out and just work as a job-hopping freeter,69 subsisting solely on part-time work.

But when the new era truly comes into play, I suspect that the current generation of twenty-somethings will be the last generation to have no particular interest in the state of society. Instead, it’ll be the young people, now in their teens, such as those reading Animage, who are forced to take an interest. It’ll happen because even the shallowest young women, who have been living without a care in the world, will be forced to confront problems like the health of their children, who increasingly have atopic eczema or nervous disorders.

When I see people who plan to get married these days, I always tell them the following: Be patient. Don’t just trust your own emotions. When you get sick of being married, don’t worry, because there will come times when you will appreciate it. So be patient, and make as many babies as you can. To live through this era together, it’s best to have lots of children. You may suffer with them if they have atopic eczema, feel threatened by AIDS, cancer, and many other things, but it’s still better to try to live with your head held high. Japan can’t unilaterally and deliberately isolate itself from the world as it did in the old sakoku days. The world’s population is exploding, but you can’t go around hysterically blaming others, pretend you can cut yourselves off from the world, or even think of getting involved in race wars. You may not like what’s happening, but just accept it, and let’s try to live together. Even if you feel angry, let’s be patient and endure, let’s try to live together. I’ve realized that this is the only way forward.

And it’s important then not to fall for some cheap nihilism or for living for the moment. Be willing to take a certain amount of risk to preserve the environment. But don’t spend too much money, or even time, on it. And make sure you do crazy things once in a while. While inhaling lots of smog, drive a two-seater convertible to work. Show them how you can drive around the filthy streets of Tokyo, collecting dust and dirt, in a car with no heater and no air conditioner, with only the clothes on your back to ward off the freezing temperatures. You must be prepared to do this.

If I can do this, I think I can probably live through the next ten years feeling good. With Porco Rosso, I feel as though I gained the means to do so.
